column3: Immediately precedes the focus by stating the same attribution to the Rahman.
Directly declares that taking a child does not befit the Rahman.
Jesus describes his own birth, death, and resurrection, locating sonship language within creaturely life.
Tests the Rahman-child formulation conditionally before rejecting its premise.
Warns against the same claim that God has taken a child.
Names Jesus son of Mary as the truth amid the dispute that leads into the rejected attribution.
Refutes divine child-taking through God's oneness, domination, and created order.
Condemns knowingly attributing false speech to God, framing the focus as fabricated ascription.
Repeats the Rahman-child claim and corrects it by identifying the alleged offspring as honored servants.
Echoes the near-rending of the heavens, supplying a close structural parallel to the surrounding response.
Exposes the inconsistency of assigning to the Rahman what the claimants themselves resent.
Condemns fabricating lies about God, the broader charge made concrete by the focus.
Directly denies that God should take a child and sets divine command as the alternative account.
Categorically denies both begetting and being begotten.
Repeats the child claim and counters it with universal divine possession and devotion.
Pairs the child claim with God's self-sufficiency and the lack of evidence or knowledge.
Denies child-taking alongside partnership and need, reinforcing divine independence.
The Annunciation presents Jesus as a pure boy bestowed by the Lord, grounding his origin in created gift rather than divine offspring.
Its unsupported promise of wealth and children forms a nearby Maryam parallel to the asserted child claim.
The recording of what the disbeliever says supplies the immediate accountability frame for unsupported speech in the same passage.
Distinguishes the valid act of invoking Allah or the Rahman from the focus's false filial attribution.
The Rahman's exclusive true kingship supplies a theological counterpoint to assigning Him a child.
